welcome_seq.preview: Not a newsletter full of tips you already know. Something more specific than that.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Glad you're here.

Steady Hound exists for one kind of person: someone who has already tried things. The diffuser. The wrap from Amazon. Possibly a behaviourist whose homework you did faithfully, and still.

If that's you, these emails are for you.

Over the next week, I'm going to tell you how Steady Hound works, why the kit is built the way it is, and what makes it different from the drawer of things that promised calm and didn't deliver it. I'll also give you something useful in most of these — not filler, just the kind of thing I'd tell you if you'd messaged me.

Today's useful thing: the single most common mistake people make when introducing an anxiety wrap is putting it on during a trigger event. Start on a quiet Tuesday morning instead. Let him sniff it. Leave it on the sofa. The slow introduction matters more than the coat itself.

More on that in the days ahead.

P.S. If you want to know what the Steady Hound kit actually is before the week is out, you can look now — I won't be offended. But if you're a reader first, stay with me.

subject_variants.subject: The problem underneath the problem
It's not October you're dreading, is it
She stopped booking weekends away. Here's why.

welcome_seq.preview: She reorganised her whole life around a dog who was struggling. Maybe you recognise this.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Most people who find Steady Hound will tell you they're looking for something to help with fireworks.

And they are. But that's not really it.

What they're actually carrying is the pre-dawn alarm so they can walk before the neighbourhood wakes up. The weekends away they stopped trying to book. The quiet, grinding belief that they are somehow failing the dog they chose to bring home.

Your dog isn't broken. He's not poorly trained or difficult. He came with a history — two years before you, in some cases more — and he's doing the only thing he knows how to do when the world gets loud and strange.

The trouble is that nothing built for standard dogs, sold in standard pet shops, accounts for any of that.

Not the one-size wrap built for a Labrador that won't sit right on a whippet chest. Not the pheromone diffuser that made the hallway smell odd and did nothing. Not the behaviourist whose methods worked in the session and nowhere else.

What would it mean to get your evenings back this October? To stop building the dread before it even arrives?

That's what I'm actually making things for.
welcome_seq.cta: Reply and tell me what October usually looks like in your house — I'm genuinely asking.

welcome_seq.preview: Twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs. And the fail rate is published.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Here's the thing about a lot of anxiety kit: it gets tested on cooperative dogs in good conditions, passed, and shipped.

Steady Hound doesn't work like that.

Every product goes through a trial panel of twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs before it goes on sale. Odd-shaped builds, dogs with history, dogs that wriggle and pace and cannot decompress in a strange environment. And the fail rate is published — the Slow-Down Feeder took three redesigns, and I say so on the listing.

That matters because you are not the first person to put this through its paces. By the time it reaches your door, it has already been through the versions that didn't work. You don't have to be the one who finds out the hard way.

The other thing that's different: every box ships with a handwritten note on how to introduce the coat slowly. Because I know — from twelve dogs and from the DMs I answer myself — that the introduction matters as much as the product.

Sizing videos for odd-shaped rescues. A real person at the other end.

Not a customer service department. Me.

P.S. The feeder redesign story is on the website if you want to read it.

subject_variants.subject: How to introduce a new coat to a nervous dog
The slow introduction: what it looks like in practice
Don't put it on at a fireworks display

welcome_seq.preview: Most people do this backwards. Here's the order that actually helps a nervous dog settle.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Today I want to give you something you can use right now, whether you have Steady Hound kit or not.

How to introduce something new to a dog that struggles with change:

Day one: leave it on the floor where he can sniff it in his own time. No pressure, no coaxing. Just there.

Day two: put it near his bed, or near where he eats. Let it become ordinary before it becomes worn.

Day three onwards: try it on for sixty seconds during something good — a calm moment after a walk, just before a meal. Take it off before he's had a chance to mind it.

Increase the time slowly, always ending before discomfort.

This is what the handwritten note in every Steady Hound box says, and it works for anything new — a coat, a bed, a feeder. The introduction done slowly is more than half the battle.

A dog who approaches something on his own terms and finds it fine is a different animal to a dog who was strapped into it cold and decided before he started that it was something to tolerate or escape.

Your dog isn't broken. He just needs the chance to come to things in his own time.

P.S. Firework season is closer than it feels. The slow introduction takes two to three weeks to do properly — there's still time, but not a lot of it.
welcome_seq.cta: Reply if you have questions about where to start with your specific dog — I'll give you a straight answer.

The price. At £58, the Settle Coat costs more than the Amazon wrap. What it doesn't do is slide off a whippet chest in forty seconds. It's been through twelve anxious rescue dogs — including odd-shaped ones — before it went on sale, and the return rate tells its own story. It also comes with a 60-night return policy. The fit. Sizing for non-standard builds is the reason the coat exists. There are sizing videos for lurchers, whippets, and staffie crosses because those are the dogs that never fit anything off the shelf. That's not marketing — it's why the product needed making.

The drawer. I know exactly which drawer you mean. If you've spent money on things that promised calm and didn't deliver it, you have every right to be sceptical. The only honest answer is: we publish the fail rate so you can see what the coat went through before it reached you. The version that arrived took the versions that didn't work. You don't have to fund the trial.

If you're still not sure, reply and tell me what's stopping you. I'll give you a straight answer, not a sales script.

subject_variants.subject: The part where I tell you about the return policy
What happens if it doesn't work for your dog
How the 60-night return actually works

promo_seq.preview: The financial risk is mine, not yours. Here's exactly how that works.
promo_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

I want to talk about what happens if this doesn't work for your dog.

The Settle Coat comes with a 60-night open return. If within 60 nights you decide it's not right — it doesn't fit, it doesn't help him settle, you change your mind entirely — you send it back and I refund you in full. No explanation required.

The same policy covers the full Calm Kit. Coat, Den Bed, Slow-Down Feeder: if any piece of it isn't right for your dog within 60 nights, return the whole kit for a full refund. What comes back muddy gets washed and donated to Otterbourne Rescue. Nothing gets binned.

On the Den Bed: if you order the wrong size for your dog's build, I'll send the correct size with a pre-paid returns label for the original. One action — no charge for the swap.

I can offer this without wincing because I made the kit for dogs that genuinely need it, sized it for odd builds, and tested it on twelve anxious rescues before it went on sale. I believe in the fail rate being published rather than hidden. I think that's the only honest way to sell something to someone who has already spent money on things that didn't work.

The risk is mine. Sixty nights is a proper test.

P.S. If you want a two-part payment on the Calm Kit — half on order, half before dispatch — reply and I'll set that up for you.

Hi {{first_name}},

It's been a while. Mid-June was the last time I was in your inbox, and I know that's longer than I'd planned.

Before I start sending again properly, I want to remind you who I am and give you a clean way out if you'd rather not hear from me.

I'm the person behind Steady Hound. I make anxiety kit for rescue dogs — a Settle Coat sized for odd-shaped builds like whippets and lurchers, a Den Bed that gives a nervous dog somewhere to decompress on his own terms, and a Slow-Down Feeder that took three redesigns before I was happy with it. Every product is tested on twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs before it goes on sale, and I publish the fail rate. I answer the DMs myself.

With bonfire season coming, I'm going to be sending more regularly for the next few weeks — useful things, honest things, and yes, some emails about what's on offer. I'd love you to stay.

But if you signed up a while ago and this isn't for you anymore, the unsubscribe link is below and I mean it kindly. No hard feelings at all.

For those staying: thank you. More soon.

P.S. If you have an anxious rescue dog and October is already on your mind, reply and tell me about your dog. I'm glad to help.
